original_summary: Coyote is a bluff-and-deduction game. Each player wears a feather card they cannot see but everyone else can. Players take turns declaring ever-higher estimates of the total of all feathers, until someone calls 'Coyote'. If the true total is below the last declaration, the declarer takes a token; otherwise the caller does. Three tokens eliminate a player, and the last survivor wins. The previous variation capped each hand at 4 turns, used a 33-card deck, forced an opening floor of 3×players and a +3 minimum raise, and made the loser open the next hand.

review.evidence: The previous variation has a structural seat edge. Testing gave these loss rates per hand: opener ≈ 0.43, turn 2 ≈ 0.12, turn 3 ≈ 0.31, turn 4 ≈ 0.14, against a fair share of 0.25. The opener is hurt by the forced floor F = 3N, which sits near the median total. Turn 3 is hurt because R9 punishes a true claim when turn 4 declares truthfully. 'Loser opens' then puts the last loser into the worst seat, so tokens snowball onto whoever lost first. No simple policy is unbeatable: always calling at turn 2 loses ≈57% and always raising the minimum at turn 4 loses ≈70%. The imbalance comes from move order, not play.

Under sensible play the loser is fixed by which band the true total falls in: below 12 the opener loses, 12–14 turn 2, 15–17 turn 3. Inside a band the stuck player loses whatever they choose, because their uncertainty is one card with SD 5.7 against a forced step of 3. About 60–70% of hand outcomes are set by the deal plus seat. The 4-turn cap stops the real Coyote contest of creeping toward the true total and judging when to stop.

Skill matters only near band edges, roughly 2 decisions per hand. Little can be learned beyond 'declare the minimum when likely true, call when likely false'. Weak players are not shut out, but strong players cannot pull away.

The hidden information is genuine: you see everyone's card but your own, and others' declarations leak information about yours. However, the +3 step, the 4-turn cap and the huge card spread (−10 to 20) leave too few turns for that leaked information to be used before the band decides the hand.
The true total, the comparison with the last declaration, the token and elimination are all arithmetic. No judge is needed.
The game is turn-based, text-only, has one hidden card per player and one shuffle per hand, and has no board. It fits the limits, though the 4-turn hand cap was a workaround that damaged the game.

problems: P1: The forced opening floor (3 × players) sits near the median total, so the opener's claim is false about 43% of the time before anyone thinks.
P2: 'Loser opens next hand' sends the loser into the worst seat, so tokens snowball onto the first unlucky player.
P3: The 4-turn cap with a turn-4 showdown (R9) punishes a TRUE claim by turn 3 and puts the end-of-hand burden on fixed seats instead of on whoever misjudges the total.
P4: The +3 minimum raise creates 3-wide 'stuck' bands in which the player to act loses whatever they choose.
P5: Card variance is too high (SD ≈ 5.7, values −10 to 20). One unseen card swamps everything that can be inferred from others' declarations.
P6: Too few decisions per hand. Reasoning acts on about 2 choices, so the deal decides most hands.

changes.what: Remove the hand turn cap. A hand passes around the table lap after lap, one lap per engine round, until someone calls Coyote. A new hand can begin only at the start of a round, and once Coyote is called the remaining turns of that round are skipped.
changes.why: This restores real Coyote. Nobody is forced to end the hand by seat. The loss lands on whoever misjudges the total, or is caught when the declaration reaches it. It also keeps choice steps at no more than 4 per round and one deal per round.

changes.what: Abolish the R9 showdown. Every hand ends with a Coyote call: the declarer loses if the true total is below the declaration, otherwise the caller loses.
changes.why: A true claim is never punished, so the only ways to lose are overclaiming or calling a true claim.

changes.what: The opener may declare any whole number from −3 to 20.
changes.why: The floor of −3 is below almost every possible total, so the opener is no longer forced into a false claim. The opener chooses how aggressive to be.

changes.what: The opener rotates one surviving seat clockwise every hand, whoever lost.
changes.why: Every player opens equally often and there is no snowball.
The 'stuck' situation shrinks to the single case where the declaration equals the true total exactly. Aiming at that exact value, and avoiding it, becomes the skill.

changes.what: Use a new 20-card deck: values −2 to 5 plus one Max→0. The card SD is about 2.0 and the 4-player total has mean ≈ 5.7.
changes.why: Your own-card uncertainty (about ±4) becomes comparable to what others' declarations reveal. Inference can narrow it, and totals are small, so hands last 1–3 laps.

changes.what: Each hand has many +1-sized decisions near the true total, made over several laps, with the full declaration history visible.
changes.why: Players can read jumps and hesitations, which carry information about their own card. They can jump to pin the next player or creep safely. This gives many reasoned decisions per hand.

keeps: Each player's own feather is hidden from them and visible to everyone else.
Strictly increasing declarations of the total of all feathers, ended by a 'Coyote!' call.
The liar-or-caller rule: the declarer loses if the total is below the declaration, otherwise the caller loses.
The special Max→0 card that cancels the highest feather.
Coyote tokens, elimination at 3 tokens, and last survivor wins.

recommendation.reason: The core of the game, inferring your own hidden card from what others see and how they declare, is excellent for training. The previous failures came from the turn cap, the opening floor, the step size and the deck, and all of these can be fixed inside the limits.

variation.name: Coyote: Around the Fire
variation.summary: Each player sees every feather but their own. Declarations of the feather total climb by at least 1 around the table, lap after lap, until someone calls Coyote. A wrong declarer or a wrong caller takes a token. The opener rotates every hand, three tokens eliminate a player, and the last survivor wins.
variation.rules:
R1 Setup. Seats are numbered 1 to N clockwise (N is 3 or 4). Every player starts with 0 tokens and is alive. opener_seat = 1, hand_active = no, round = 1.

R2 Deck. The deck has exactly 20 cards:
- one −2
- two −1
- three 0
- three 1
- three 2
- three 3
- two 4
- two 5
- one special card, Max→0

R3 Start of a round. If hand_active is no, a new hand begins:
- The deck is restored to all 20 cards and shuffled.
- Each alive player is dealt exactly 1 card face-down.
- Each player is privately told the card of every other alive player, never their own.
- current_declaration is set to none and hand_active to yes.
- Everyone is told that a new hand begins and who opens it.
If hand_active is already yes, the hand in progress simply continues.

R4 Turn order. In every round the alive players take exactly one turn each:
- The first turn goes to the player in opener_seat, then each next alive player clockwise, so a round has as many turns as there are alive players (at most 4).
- The order is the same in every round of a hand, so a hand passes around the table lap after lap.
- If Coyote is called, the hand ends and any remaining turns of that round are skipped.
Before each turn, all players are shown the current declaration, who made it, and every declaration made so far this hand.

R5 A turn.
(a) If there is no declaration yet this hand, the player must declare a whole number from −3 to 20.
(b) Otherwise the player either declares a whole number at least current_declaration + 1 and at most 20, or calls Coyote. If current_declaration is 20, the player must call Coyote.
(c) A declaration makes that player the current declarer and the number the current declaration.

R6 True total. All cards are revealed to everyone.
- Add all card values, counting Max→0 as 0.
- If Max→0 was dealt, the single highest other dealt card counts as 0 instead, provided its value is positive. If several cards tie for highest, only one of them is cancelled.

R7 Resolving Coyote. Compute the true total.
- If the true total is less than the current declaration, the current declarer loses the hand.
- Otherwise the caller loses the hand.
The loser gains 1 token. All cards, the true total and the loser are announced to everyone. hand_active becomes no.

R8 Elimination. A player with 3 tokens is eliminated. They receive no more cards and are skipped in turn order.

R9 Next opener. After every hand, opener_seat moves to the next alive player clockwise from the current opener, whoever lost. If the current opener was just eliminated, it moves to the next alive player clockwise from their seat.

R10 End. The game ends immediately when only one player is alive, and that player wins. If round 40 ends first, any unfinished hand is discarded without a token. The alive player with the fewest tokens then wins; if two or more alive players tie for fewest, the game is a draw.

There is no table talk: declarations and calls are the only communication.
variation.objective: Be the last player not eliminated (3 tokens eliminate). If 40 rounds pass with more than one player alive, the alive player with the fewest tokens wins, and a tie for fewest is a draw.

balanced.evidence:
Deck check: -10 + 2(-5) + 3(0) + 4(1+2+3+4+5) + 3(10) + 2(15) + 20 + Max->0 = 33 cards with total value 120, so the mean card is about 3.6. The lowest possible true total with 5 cards is -10-5-5+0+0 = -20, and with fewer cards it is higher. Any declaration of -21 or less is therefore always true. Opener declarations go down to -30.

Thoughtless policy 'always declare the minimum legal number (current+1)':
- Opener declares -30.
- R1 declares -29.
- R2 declares -28.
- R3 is forced by R5 to call_coyote. The true total is at least -20, which is at least -28, so the caller loses.

Winner-rule table for one hand, with the policy holder in the first or second response:
- If the opponent raises after them, they are no longer current declarer and cannot lose.
- If the opponent calls after their declaration of -21 or less, the caller loses.
- If the third responder is forced to call, the third responder loses.
- Result: the policy NEVER loses a hand from the R1 or R2 seat, whatever anyone else does.
The opener declaring -30 also never loses: a caller loses, and a raiser takes over as declarer.

The only player who can lose is the forced third responder, and they lose with certainty. The hand loser is fixed by seat:
- 3 survivors: the responders are 2, 3, then the opener, so the opener loses. The loser re-opens (R9), loses again, and is eliminated after 3 hands.
- 2 survivors: the order is A then B, A, B, so B loses. B re-opens, then A loses. The tokens simply alternate.
- 4-5 survivors: seat opener+3 loses every hand, a deterministic rotation.

No one ever has a reason to bid high, so the cards are irrelevant. Seat position decides everything. A strictly safe option exists, so the game fails.

playable.evidence:
The rules are complete and unambiguous.
- Deck composition, the 1-card deal, the visibility rule and the Max->0 resolution (including ties and the 'only if positive' case) are all specified.
- Bidding has a 60 cap, and the forced call means every hand ends within 4 choices.
- R10 bound: four eliminated players at 3 tokens each plus the winner at up to 2 tokens gives 14 hands. This is correct and within the 40-round limit.
- Complexity is within limits: 16 steps (max 20), 4 choice steps (max 4: opener plus 3 responses), 18 attributes (max 20), 1 hidden element, 1 draw per round.
- Everything is decided by arithmetic, needs no judge or board, and is turn-based. Sequential bidding is appropriate because order is the point.
- Omitting talk is defensible: the declarations are the communication, and free talk would only add words.

Minor oddities, not failures:
- With 5 survivors, the seat just before the opener never acts in that hand.
- The sentence 'The deck size after a finished hand is not a measure of dealing' is odd but harmless.
- The third response is a one-option 'choice'.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Under the intended good strategy, every R1, R2 and opener player declares -21 or less, which can never be false. The third responder loses with certainty. The loser of every hand is therefore fixed by seating and the R9 opener rule:
- Cards play no role.
- There is nothing to infer about one's own card.
- There is no opponent to model, since no declaration ever approaches the true total.

Chance share is about 0%, and reasoning share is about 0%. The outcome is mechanical from turn order. The original game's core inference (estimating your unseen card from the visible sum, about V + 3.6, and judging whether a bid near the true total is a bluff) is never exercised. A good reasoner is not favoured over a minimum-bidder; both get identical results.

required_changes: Remove the forced call. The third responder must choose between call_coyote and declaring a higher number. If they declare, the hand resolves immediately with the opener as caller, so the last declarer is exposed to a check. This stays within 4 choice steps.

Add a floor so declarations must reflect the cards. The opener must declare at least the sum of the cards they can see (the game knows this number). Every raise must be at least 3 higher than current_declaration. After three raises the declaration then typically exceeds the true total (visible sum plus about 3.6), so calling becomes a live, inference-driven choice and no 'always safe' bid exists.
Alternatively, raise the opener minimum to at least 0 and the minimum raise to 4. This removes the guaranteed-true region below -20.
With 5 survivors, state explicitly that the seat before the opener sits out. Or rotate which responders act, so that every player bids over the game and seat position gives no systematic edge.
Re-check with the new rules that no policy among always-minimum, always-call or always-maximum avoids losing against both sensible and random play.

balanced.evidence:
DECK NUMBERS. 33 cards, values sum to 120 (Max→0 counts as 0). Card mean = 120/33 ≈ 3.64. E[x²] = 1520/33 ≈ 46.1, so card SD ≈ 5.7. Max→0 is dealt with probability about 4/33 ≈ 0.12 in a 4-player hand and cancels the highest other card (about 9 on average), costing about 1.1. Four-card true total: mean ≈ 13.4, SD ≈ 11. Three-card true total: mean ≈ 10.1, SD ≈ 9.5. Your uncertainty is your own card only: K + own, SD 5.7, while declarations must step by 3.

WHERE THE LOSS LANDS (4 players, F = 12, everyone playing sensibly). Each band is followed by its probability and the player who loses.
- Total < 12 (≈ 43%). The opener must declare at least 12, so the claim is already false. Turn 2 calls and wins, and the opener loses. Turn 2 cannot safely declare 15 either, because turn 3 would call.
- Total 12–14 (≈ 10%). Turn 2 is stuck: calling loses because true ≥ 12, and declaring 15 loses to turn 3's call. Turn 2 loses.
- Total 15–17 (≈ 10%). Turn 3 is stuck: calling loses because true ≥ 15, and declaring 18 loses to turn 4's call. Turn 3 loses.
- Total ≥ 18 (≈ 35%). Turn 3 must declare D3. Turn 4 calls if true < D3 and declares D3+3 if true ≥ D3+3. Turn 3 escapes only if true lands in [D3, D3+2]. The best 3-value own-card window, for example {1,2,3} or {3,4,5}, holds 12/33 ≈ 36%. So turn 3 loses about 60% of this band and turn 4 the rest.
- Approximate loss rates per hand: opener ≈ 0.43, turn 2 ≈ 0.12, turn 3 ≈ 0.31, turn 4 ≈ 0.14. A fair share is 0.25. The 3-player case is the same: F = 9 against a mean of ≈ 10.1, so P(total < F) ≈ 45% and the opener absorbs it.

SEAT EDGE AND SNOWBALL. R13 makes the loser the next opener. Losing a hand therefore puts you in the seat that loses about 43% of hands, and you lose about 1.7× as often as a fair share. Tokens snowball onto whoever lost first. This is a structural seat edge set by move order, not by play.

R9 ALSO PUNISHES A TRUE CLAIM. When turn 4 declares and true ≥ D4, the turn-3 player loses even though their own claim D3 < D4 was true. That is the source of turn 3's narrow escape window.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (none dominates, but this does not rescue the seat imbalance).
- Always call at turn 2: loses whenever true ≥ D1 = 12, ≈ 57% of hands.
- Always declare the minimum: at turn 4 it declares D3+3 ≥ 21 and loses when true < 21, ≈ 70%.
- Always call at turn 4: loses when true ≥ D3 ≥ 18, ≈ 35%.
- No option is strictly dominant, and both or all players can still win. The check fails on the opener and loser-opens edge.

playable.evidence:
LIMITS. Stated 18 steps (≤ 20), 4 choice steps (≤ 4), 14 attributes (≤ 20), 1 hidden element (own card, ≤ 3), 1 random draw per round (one shuffle-and-deal, ≤ 1), at most 11 rounds (≤ 40). All within limits.

LENGTH. The arithmetic checks out: 4 players gives 9 tokens to eliminate three players plus at most 2 on the winner, so 11 hands. 3 players gives 6 + 2 = 8 hands. The game is finite and always yields one winner.

RULES ARE COMPLETE.
- The early stop after a call at turn 2 or 3 is done with per-step `when` conditions on the later choice steps. It is a flat list, not a block substitution.
- R8 and R9 are a single conditional resolution.
- Max→0 is arithmetic, and the tie-break is irrelevant to the sum.
- Turn order is defined for 4, 3 and 2 survivors.
- The cap of 80 and the 'only calling allowed' case are covered.
- Elimination skipping and the opener after an eliminated loser are defined.
- Seeing everyone's card but your own is a hidden-hand view the engine supports.
- No board, clock, judge or trading is needed.

TALK. There is no talk phase. Players do disagree, since exactly one loses, but the declarations themselves are a public, costly signal about cards each player cannot see. Players are not reduced to guessing each other, so the absence is acceptable. Explicitly stating 'no talk' would be cleaner.

REPEATED-GAME CHECK. This is an elimination game, not highest-total, so the late-round betrayal check does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT THERE IS TO INFER. There is real inference: others see your card, so their declarations leak information about it.

WHY CHANCE DOMINATES.
- With sensible play, the hand's loser is essentially fixed by which band the true total falls in, and that comes from the deal: <12 → opener; 12–14 → turn 2; 15–17 → turn 3.
- In the ≥18 band, turn 3 survives only if their unseen card lands in a 3-wide window (≤ 36%).
- Inside a band, the stuck player loses whatever they choose. Their remaining uncertainty is their own card, SD 5.7, against a step of 3.
- Skill matters only near band edges and in reading others' declarations. Those are only about 2 decisions per hand, with little room because the minimum step is 3 and there are only 4 turns.

ROUGH SHARE. About 60–70% of hand outcomes are fixed by the deal plus seat, not by decisions.

ALL-GOOD-PLAY TEST. When every player plays the intended strategy (declare the minimum when true is likely above it, call when it is likely below), the loser each hand is the player sitting at the band the deal produced. Because the loser then opens and the opener loses ≈ 43%, the first unlucky deal tends to cascade. A good reasoner is not clearly favoured over a mediocre one.

required_changes: Remove the forced opening floor: let the opener declare any whole number from −20 to 80, or set F = 0, so the opener is not pushed above the median total about 43% of the time.
Replace 'loser opens' (R13) with a fixed rotation: the opener moves one surviving seat clockwise each hand. This removes the snowball onto the worst seat.
Change the minimum raise from +3 to +1, so 'stuck' bands shrink to a single value and outcomes depend on judging the total, not on which 3-wide band the deal hit.

Fix R9 so a true lower claim is not punished. If the turn-4 declaration is true (true ≥ D4), the player with the lowest declaration this hand loses only if it was also the furthest below the true total. Simpler: make turn 4 call-only, so every hand ends in an R8 call.

Reduce own-card variance so reasoning outweighs the deal: remove the −10 and 20 and one 15, or tell each player privately one coarse fact about their own card (e.g. whether it is ≥ 3) as a single hidden element.

balanced.evidence: Deck check: the numbered cards sum to -2-1-1+0+3+6+9+8+10 = 32 over 19 cards, a mean of about 1.68 and an SD of about 1.8. Max->0 cancels the highest positive card. Extremes: the 3-player minimum total is -2-1-1 = -4. The 4-player maximum is 5+5+4+4 = 18, so a declaration of 20 is never true. Each player sees every card except their own, so every player has the same one-card uncertainty and no seat has an information edge. WINNER-RULE TESTS. (1) ALWAYS CALL: the opener can open at -3, which loses only if the total is -4, a very rare deal. Any declarer who sees others' sum S can declare about S-2, which is wrong only in rare cases (holding -2, or Max->0 cancelling a card). So always-call loses almost every hand it calls and is eliminated quickly. Against random declarers it wins only when they overbid. (2) ALWAYS HIGHEST (declare 20): the truth is at most 18 < 20. This declarer loses every hand, because the next player is forced to call under R5b. (3) ALWAYS MINIMUM RAISE, never call: it is safe only while the declaration stays at or below the truth. Once the ladder passes the truth, the min-raiser keeps raising into a false number and is called. A sensible player who expects the total to be about T can jump to T, so that the min-raiser must declare T+1 or more and lose. Min-raise therefore loses whenever the ladder reaches it near the top, which happens regularly. (4) Always pass is not an option. No action is strictly dominant. Declaring D is safe only if D is at most the truth, and calling is right only if the declaration exceeds the truth. The best move therefore depends on your hidden card and on reading other players' bids. Seat edge: the opener bids first but can bid low and safe. Later players gain information from earlier bids but face a higher ladder. R9 rotates the opener every hand, so over the 6 to 11 hands every seat opens about equally. Every player can win. Both elimination and the round-40 fewest-tokens fallback are reachable. No labelled payoff ordering exists to contradict.

playable.evidence: The rules cover: setup; the deck; the deal; private views; legal declarations (opening -3 to 20, a raise of at least 1, a forced call at 20); the true total, including Max->0 ties and non-positive cases; resolution; elimination; opener rotation, including an eliminated opener; hands that span rounds; and the round-40 cutoff with a draw on a tie. Minor gap: the round counter increment is implied, not stated, but the meaning is clear. Finite: at most 40 rounds. Each hand ends within 24 declarations, because the range is -3 to 20 and every raise is at least 1. The result is decided by arithmetic on cards and token counts. Limits: 14 steps of 20; 4 choice steps (one per alive player) of 4; 13 attributes of 20; 1 hidden element (own card) of 3; 1 random draw (the shuffle and deal, only at a hand start) of 1; 40 rounds of 40. Uses supported features: hidden_hands, private_channel to show each player the others' cards, sequential_choice, numeric_bids, elimination, variable_player_count. Sequential turns are correct here because declarations must escalate in order, so the order is the point. No board, clock, judge, trading or binding agreements are needed. Talk is omitted, which is sensible. Interests conflict, but each declaration already encodes what the bidder sees, including your own card, so players reason from actions rather than guessing. Free talk would mostly add cheap bluffing. The original Coyote also has no talk. The repeated-cooperation test does not apply because this is not a cooperation game.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: There is something to infer: your own card, from others' declarations. Worked example (3 players, cards A=1, B=3, C=5, true total 9). A sees 8 and expects about 9.7. B sees 6 and expects about 7.7. C sees 4 and expects about 5.7. A opens 8, which is safe unless A holds a negative card or a cancelling Max->0. A naive B trusts his own 7.7 estimate, calls, and loses, since 9 >= 8. A reasoning B infers that A sees B+C of about 8. Since B knows C=5, he deduces that his own card is about 3, and raises instead. Inference thus turns the one-card uncertainty into near-knowledge. Sizing a bid, or jumping to exactly the estimated total, puts pressure on the next player, which rewards planning and opponent modelling. Chance: the deal decides whose card is extreme (5 or -2), which biases that player's estimate by up to about 3 points. Good players partly correct this by reading bids. I estimate that about 30 to 40 percent of a single hand's outcome is down to the deal. The game needs 6 to 11 hands, and 3 tokens to eliminate a player, so luck averages out. When all play well, the loser of each hand varies with the deal, but no hidden type fixes the overall winner. Players who read declarations well are clearly favoured over naive estimators or fixed policies.
